pathogen_scientific_name.quote: C. musae is the most common species associated with anthracnose of banana and has been widely accepted as the causal agent of the disease

type_of_disease.quote: Species of fungus Colletotrichum musae Scientific classification Kingdom: Fungi

affected_parts.quote: Besides causing anthracnose on banana fruits, C. musae can also infect the bracts, flowers, petioles and leaves of banana plants ( Jones & Slabaugh 1998 ).

summary.value: Anthracnose of banana appears as black, sunken lesions on the fruit, with spore masses or acervuli within the lesions; dark brown/black lesions on green fruit increase in size on yellow fruit with orange fungal growth in the centre; symptoms can also occur on the tips of fruit and are associated with premature ripening.
summary.quote: Symptoms of anthracnose include black and sunken lesions with spore masses or acervuli in the lesion.

diagnostic_features.value: Black and sunken lesions bearing spore masses or acervuli in the lesion; on yellow fruit, orange fungal growth develops in the centre of enlarging lesions; disease becomes severe where fruit is wounded by scratches during handling and transportation.
diagnostic_features.quote: Anthracnose becomes severe when the banana fruits are wounded by scratches during handling and transportation, making the fruit unmarketable.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Scientific Name Banana bunchy top nanavirus. The abbreviatiion is BBTV.

type_of_disease.quote: BBT is caused by a virus.

affected_parts.quote: Plants with banana bunchy top (BBT) have narrow, progressively shorter leaves with little distance between them, hence the name 'bunchy top'

summary.value: Infected plants are stunted with narrow, progressively shorter, bunched leaves that have upward-rolling, yellow margins, and the minor leaf veins show short dark-green dots and dashes forming downward-curving hooks near the midrib.
summary.quote: Plants with banana bunchy top (BBT) have narrow, progressively shorter leaves with little distance between them, hence the name 'bunchy top'. Leaf edges often roll upwards with yellow margins.

diagnostic_features.value: Short, dark-green dots and dashes along the minor leaf veins ('Morse-code' patterns) that form hooks curving downwards near the edge of the midrib, best seen by holding the leaf up to the light and viewing from the underside.
diagnostic_features.quote: The most characteristic symptoms are short, dark-green dots and dashes along the minor leaf veins, so-called 'Morse-code' patterns, which form hooks curving downwards near the edge of the midrib (Photo 3). Hold the leaf up to the light and view from the underside.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: The cigar end rot disease (Trachysphaera fructigena)

type_of_disease.quote: It is a fungal disease that can attack the ripening fruit of banana

affected_parts.quote: causing a dry rot of the flower end that produces an ash grey wrinkled lesion similar to the burnt end of a cigar

summary.value: A dry rot of the flower (cigar) end of ripening banana fruit producing an ash grey wrinkled lesion resembling the burnt end of a cigar; in storage or transport it may progress to involve the whole fruit.
summary.quote: causing a dry rot of the flower end that produces an ash grey wrinkled lesion similar to the burnt end of a cigar. In storage or during transport the disease may progress to involve the whole fruit. Symptoms are: lesions, abnormal shape, visible mould.

diagnostic_features.value: Corrugated affected tissues covered with conidiophores and powdery grey conidia resembling ash on a cigar end, with blackening and shrinkage of the skin at the fruit tip, and dry fibrous rot in the pulp.
diagnostic_features.quote: The affected tissues are corrugated and covered with conidiophores and powdery grey conidia resembling ash on a cigar end. Dry rot also occurs in the pulp and the affected tissues become dry and fibrous.

conflicts.note: TNAU Agritech attributes cigar end rot to Verticillium theobromae; Infonet Biovision attributes it to Trachysphaera fructigena. Both pathogens are reported in the literature as causes of cigar end rot. No taxonomy validation was available; Trachysphaera fructigena is used as canonical as it is the more widely cited primary pathogen.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Causal agents Neocordana musae and Neocordana johnstonii

type_of_disease.quote: It is caused by two Neocordana fungi that are often found as secondary invaders of leaf lesions caused by other fungi.

affected_parts.quote: The most characteristic symptoms of the disease are on the leaf.

summary.value: Large, pale brown, oval to fusiform necrotic leaf lesions with pale grey concentric ring patterns, a dark brown border, and a bright yellow halo; lesions often coalesce into large necrotic patches and leaves ultimately turn brown and dry out.
summary.quote: They are large, pale brown, oval to fusiform necrotic lesions with pale grey concentric ring patterns, with a dark brown border surrounded by a bright yellow halo separating the lesion from the healthy leaf tissue. Often, lesions coalesce into large necrotic patches. The leaves ultimately turn brown and dry out.

diagnostic_features.value: Pale grey concentric ring patterns within the lesion, a dark brown border, and a bright yellow halo separating the lesion from healthy tissue; lesions caused by N. musae are larger and oval to elliptical, while those caused by N. johnstonii are smaller and more fusiform with age; spores produced on the underside of leaves cause lesions to appear greyish-brown and hairy.
diagnostic_features.quote: with a dark brown border surrounded by a bright yellow halo separating the lesion from the healthy leaf tissue. The leaf spots caused by N. musae are larger and oval to elliptical in shape, while those caused by N. johnstonii are generally smaller and become more fusiform with age.

look_alikes.quote: When the infection is associated with other diseases, e.g. with black leaf streak, the lesions are enlarged and become necrotic.

conflicts.note: Bayer Crop Science uses the older names Cordana musae and Cordana johnstonii, noting Neocordana as synonyms. The current accepted names are Neocordana musae and Neocordana johnstonii per ProMusa and Wikipedia.

affected_parts.quote: This disease, characterized by rot and necrosis, affects tissues joining the fingers with each other, called the crown. It may reach the pedicel and even the banana pulp when crown rot is severe.

summary.value: Crown rot is characterized by rot and necrosis affecting the crown tissues that join the banana fingers; in severe cases it extends to the pedicel and the banana pulp. Symptoms are usually invisible at packing and develop during shipment, ripening, and storage.
summary.quote: This disease, characterized by rot and necrosis, affects tissues joining the fingers with each other, called the crown. It may reach the pedicel and even the banana pulp when crown rot is severe.

diagnostic_features.value: Rot and necrosis of the tissues joining the fingers (the crown), potentially reaching the pedicel and banana pulp; usually invisible when fruits are packed and appearing during shipment, ripening, and storage.
diagnostic_features.quote: Usually invisible when the fruits are packed for transportation from tropical countries to distant destinations, disease symptoms occur during shipment, ripening, and storage. This disease, characterized by rot and necrosis, affects tissues joining the fingers with each other, called the crown.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: PATHOGEN: Mycosphaerella fijiensis - found in nearly all the world's banana-growing regions.

type_of_disease.quote: The fungus was first described in 1969 by Morelet on specimens from Fiji.

affected_parts.quote: The first symptoms of black Sigatoka disease are tiny, chlorotic spots that appear on the bottom (abaxial) surface of the 3rd or 4th open leaf.

summary.value: Tiny chlorotic spots appear on the underside of young leaves, growing into thin brown vein-limited streaks that darken (sometimes with a purple tinge), enlarge into fusiform or elliptical lesions, and coalesce into characteristic black streaking and water-soaked, blackened leaf areas bearing tiny black globose fruiting bodies.
summary.quote: The first symptoms of black Sigatoka disease are tiny, chlorotic spots that appear on the bottom (abaxial) surface of the 3rd or 4th open leaf. The spots grow into thin brown streaks that are limited by leaf veins. The color of the streaks becomes darker, sometimes with a purple tinge, and visible on the top (adaxial) surface. The lesions then enlarge, becoming fusiform or elliptical, and darken to give the characteristic black streaking of the leaves

diagnostic_features.value: Black color in the young streaks and spots, absence of a distinct yellow halo (unlike yellow Sigatoka); conidiophores produced singly or in small groups (not in large sporodochial clusters) with a distinct basal scar on conidium and conidiophore; dark streaks appear on leaf numbers 2–4 of unsprayed Cavendish.
diagnostic_features.quote: It has black color in the young streaks and spots and lacks the distinct yellow halo that is present in young streaks of yellow Sigatoka.

look_alikes.quote: Although the lesions of yellow Sigatoka ( Mycosphaerella musicola ) may look similar, one can distinguish between the yellow and black Sigatokas by examining conidiophore structure
